options: has real eigenvalues and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors
questions.explanation: A real symmetric matrix is orthogonally diagonalizable over the reals, so its eigenvalues are real and its eigenvectors can be chosen orthonormal. A non-real eigenvalue can occur for a real matrix that is not symmetric. The identity is symmetric and its only eigenvalue is 1. Symmetry allows nonzero off-diagonal entries.

questions.prompt: What is the larger eigenvalue of \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\)?
questions.explanation: The characteristic polynomial is \(\lambda^2 - 8\lambda + 12 = (\lambda-6)(\lambda-2)\). The larger root is 6. The trace 8 is the sum of the two eigenvalues, the determinant 12 is their product, and 4 is a diagonal entry rather than an eigenvalue.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>symmetric 2 by 2 matrix</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">4   2</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2   4</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with equal diagonal entries and equal off-diagonal entries.

questions.prompt: If the columns of \(U\) are orthonormal eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix \(A\), and \(D\) holds the eigenvalues, then
options: \(A = D U\), with no further factor
\(A = U D\) and the transpose is optional
questions.explanation: Orthonormal columns mean \(U^{-1} = U^T\), so the factorization is \(A = U D U^T\). Adding \(U\) and \(D\) is not a change of basis. Dropping \(U^T\) leaves the coordinates in the eigenbasis.

options: is not an eigenvector, because its entries differ
questions.explanation: \(A(1,-1) = (2,-2) = 2(1,-1)\). The eigenvalue 6 belongs to \((1,1)\), since \(A(1,1) = (6,6)\). The diagonal entry 4 is not that stretch factor.

questions.explanation: \(\det A = 16 - 4 = 12\), which is also the product of the eigenvalues 6 and 2. The trace is 8, and the off-diagonal entry 2 is not the determinant.

questions.explanation: The trace is \(4+4 = 8\), the same as the sum of the eigenvalues 6 and 2. Their difference is 4, and the off-diagonal entries are not part of the trace.

questions.prompt: In the factorization \(A = U D U^T\) of a symmetric matrix, the three factors
options: translate the vector, then stretch it
stretch in the original coordinates, then rotate twice the same way
add the eigenvalues to the vector
rotate into the eigenbasis, stretch each coordinate by its eigenvalue, and rotate back
questions.explanation: \(U^T\) writes the vector in the eigenbasis, \(D\) multiplies each coordinate by its eigenvalue, and \(U\) returns to the original coordinates. There is no translation. Unequal eigenvalues stretch different directions by different factors.

questions.prompt: Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(x = (2, 0)\). What is \(x^T A x\)?
questions.explanation: Only the first coordinate is nonzero, so \(x^T A x = 5 \cdot 2^2 = 20\). Using the other eigenvalue would give 4. Forgetting to square the coordinate would give 10.

questions.explanation: \(A(0,1) = (0,1)\), so the eigenvalue is 1. The other diagonal entry, 5, belongs to \((1,0)\). The trace 6 is the sum of the two eigenvalues.

questions.prompt: A symmetric matrix is positive definite when
options: its trace is positive, even if an eigenvalue is negative
its determinant is positive and nothing else is required
questions.explanation: For a symmetric matrix, positive definiteness is exactly the condition that every eigenvalue is positive. A positive trace or a positive determinant can hold while an eigenvalue is negative. Positive entries do not control the eigenvalues.

questions.prompt: The symmetric matrix \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\) has eigenvalues 6 and 2, both positive. What is its largest singular value?
questions.explanation: On a positive semidefinite matrix the singular values are the eigenvalues. The largest is 6. The smaller eigenvalue 2 is the other singular value, and the trace 8 is not a singular value.

questions.prompt: The Rayleigh quotient \(x^T A x / x^T x\) of a symmetric matrix, evaluated at an eigenvector,
questions.explanation: If \(Ax = \lambda x\) and \(x \ne 0\), then \(x^T A x = \lambda\, x^T x\), so the quotient equals \(\lambda\). The trace and the determinant are the sum and the product of all the eigenvalues, not the value on one eigenvector.
